newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Krupp bids 13.6 billion marks for Thyssen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Krupp bids 13.6 billion marks for Thyssen.

text.p: German industry giant Krupp launched a rare 13.6 billion mark ($8 billion) hostile takeover bid for its larger rival Thyssen AG on Tuesday, offering 435 marks a share, 25 percent over Monday's closing price.

The merger would create Europe's third largest steel company with annual turnover of some 63 billion marks ($37.3 billion), and could spark further industry consolidation as it challenges its larger European competitors Usinor Sacilor of France and British Steel Plc.

Thyssen shares, which were suspended from regular trade but still changing hands in unofficial trade, leapt to a new high of 410 marks immediately after the news. Krupp shares, meanwhile, were at about 270 marks, two marks below their last official close on Monday.

The offer announcement sparked an angry response from Thyssen, caught off guard by the unexpected grab for control. Thyssen recommended that shareholders do nothing while it prepared its response to the unwelcome bid.
Steel workers fearing massive lay-offs downed tools in angry protest throughout the Ruhr Valley, Germany's industrial heartland.

Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp chief Gerhard Cromme, dubbed the "job killer" after his spectacular 1991 takeover of Hoesch that resulted in over 20,000 job cuts, was booed by steel workers at Krupp offices as he tried to explain the takeover.
Speaking behind a wall of bullet-proof riot shields over the din of shouting workers, Cromme dismissed Thyssen's allegations that a takeover would cost "tens of thousands" of jobs.

"The numbers that are making the rounds are nothing but panic-mongering," he said, adding that it made sense in the interest of retaining competitive jobs in the Ruhr to forge a larger union of Germany's top two steel companies.

While Thyssen and union officials slammed the Krupp bid as "Wild West tactics" alien to German corporate culture, Deutsche Bank AG management board member Rolf Breuer said it was the shape of things to come.
The offer showed German industry was entering a phase of stronger concentration ahead of European economic and monetary union, said Breuer, who will take over as Deutsche chief executive in May.
Breuer said he was very interested to see that the Thyssen takeover proceed in an orderly fashion like takeovers in Britain and the United States, where such deals are common.

"I ... hope that it demonstrates that the German financial centre is also in a position to carry out a takeover in a manner that is common in other countries," he told a news conference on asset management.
Deutsche Bank's investment arm Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, Dresdner Bank, U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs and other unidentified institutions were financing the Krupp bid.

Hermann Reith, analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt, said it would be difficult for Thyssen to fight the offer. "It will be critical for Thyssen to make its shareholders believe that the company is worth more than this amount.

Reith said he valued Thyssen shares at about 370 marks on core units and after the divestment of loss-making units. But its stake in the e-plus mobile phone network added another 80 marks or so to the share price and real estate reserves added another minimum 20 marks per share, he said.
Krupp may be planning to sell the e-plus stake to finance at least part of the purchase of its larger rival.
Peter Fish, an industry analyst at MEPS in Sheffield, England, said rationalisation was needed at both firms and that could only occur by making bigger units, particularly in Germany.

But such analysis is little comfort to workers who see only the human cost in lost jobs and the massive shifting of social and economic structures in the country's industrial heartland. German unemployment is at its highest level since 1933.

Around 1,000 Thyssen steel workers protested at the Krupp headquarters. Some attempted to charge the building while others threw eggs and oranges at the Krupp chairman shouting "Where is the killer?" and "Come out, Cromme!"
In Dortmund, where Krupp's steel activities are based at the former Hoesch Stahl plant, its own steel workers joined protests.

The takeover could face political hurdles as government officials fear another round of explosive protests just days after thousands of German miners marched on Bonn, blocking streets and disrupting government business to protest against cuts in subsidies to the coal industry.

The European Commission said it had not been notified by Germany's Federal Cartel Office of a Krupp-Thyssen merger, but European Union sources said a merger of the two steel giants would surely be reviewed by the EU.
